By raising the federal funds target to 3.75–4% and signaling “ongoing increases” while continuing balance-sheet runoff, the FOMC adopts a deliberately restrictive stance to re-anchor inflation expectations—broadly in line with Taylor-rule prescriptions when inflation is above target and with the literature on central bank credibility and independence (Taylor; Bernanke & Mihov; Romer & Romer). The explicit attention to the “cumulative tightening” and the “lags” of policy transmission reflects the Brainard conservatism principle and evidence that contractionary policy shocks weigh on activity with delays (Romer & Romer). Quantitative tightening via Treasuries and agency MBS caps should also put upward pressure on term premia consistent with term-structure findings (Cochrane–Piazzesi). While supply-side forces—including the war in Ukraine—continue to add to inflation, the stated commitment to 2% and the use of rates, forward guidance, and balance-sheet tools are supportive of medium-term disinflation, albeit at the cost of softer near-term growth and tighter financial conditions.
